title: The Battle Before The Battle
subtitle: Leaving a Legacy
tagline: Infrastructure can be inherited. Conviction has to be taught.
headline: Leaving a Legacy
headline_sub: When the Next Generation Inherits Something Healthier
seo_title: Leaving a Legacy: What the Next Generation Inherits
seo_description: Psalm 78 calls one generation to tell the next what God has done. How leaders and fathers pass on conviction, not just structures, and prepare others to carry it forward.
keywords: passing faith to the next generation

scriptures.text: We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done.

so the next generation would know them, even the children yet to be born, and they in turn would tell their children. Then they would put their trust in God and would not forget his deeds but would keep his commands.
After that whole generation had been gathered to their ancestors, another generation grew up who knew neither the LORD nor what he had done for Israel.

blocks.text: Psalm 78 calls God’s people to tell the next generation about His deeds, so their children will put their trust in Him and keep His commands.
Judges 2 describes a later generation that knew neither the Lord nor what He had done for Israel.
Psalm 78 looks forward.
Judges 2 looks at a devastating reality.
Together they raise a generational question:
WHAT HAPPENS WHEN ONE GENERATION EXPERIENCES GOD’S FAITHFULNESS BUT THE NEXT DOES NOT TRULY KNOW HIM?
Psalm 78 doesn’t merely tell parents to preserve information.
It connects remembering God’s works with trust, obedience, and hope.
The purpose of telling the story is formation.

items: Not nostalgia.
Not institutional pride.
Not simply preserving a family or national identity.

blocks.text: The next generation must learn where to place its trust.
“IF WE BUILD SOMETHING SUCCESSFUL, THE NEXT GENERATION WILL AUTOMATICALLY BENEFIT.”
Imagine a founder who builds a thriving organization.

items: The finances are strong.
The reputation is excellent.
The programs are effective.

blocks.text: But nobody understands the convictions that shaped its earliest decisions.
The founder leaves.
A new generation inherits the structures without understanding the principles.

items: They know what was built, but not why.
They know the procedures, but not the wisdom.
They know the accomplishments, but not the dependence on God.

blocks.text: Now bring it home.
Imagine a father who passes on the rules and the routines. Church on Sunday. Grace before dinner. Work hard. Don’t quit.
But he never tells his kids what God actually did for him. The night he almost walked away. The prayer God answered. The mercy that met him.
His children inherit the habits without ever hearing the story.
AN ORGANIZATION, OR A FAMILY, CAN PASS FORWARD ITS STRUCTURE WITHOUT PASSING FORWARD ITS CONVICTIONS.
Why does this happen?
Because building is demanding.

items: Leaders become consumed with today’s responsibilities.
Developing successors takes time.
Explaining decisions requires patience.
Sharing authority can feel uncomfortable.

blocks.text: And sometimes a leader quietly enjoys being indispensable.
But the next generation cannot inherit wisdom that nobody intentionally teaches.
Nor can it mature if it is never entrusted with responsibility.
THE BATTLE BEGINS WHEN PRESERVING MY IMPORTANCE BECOMES MORE ATTRACTIVE THAN PREPARING SOMEONE ELSE.
FAITHFUL LEADERSHIP THINKS BEYOND ITS OWN TENURE.
Psalm 78 calls for intentional transmission.

items: Tell the story.
Explain God’s faithfulness.
Teach His commands.
Help the next generation put its hope in Him.

blocks.text: Judges 2 warns us that continuity cannot be assumed.
Yet one distinction matters.
Parents and leaders can teach faithfully without controlling another person’s response.
Faith is not mechanically inherited.
The next generation remains responsible for its own response to God.
Our calling is not to guarantee outcomes.
It is to steward what we have been entrusted to teach.

items: What are we passing on besides buildings, budgets, and programs?
Who understands why our organization, or our family, exists?
Who knows the convictions behind our decisions?
Are younger leaders being developed, or merely assigned tasks?
What wisdom are we withholding because sharing it threatens our importance?
Will the next generation inherit our faithfulness, or merely the machinery we built?

blocks.text: Identify one person you can intentionally develop.

items: Share the story behind your work.
Explain the convictions that guide your decisions.
Invite questions.
Transfer responsibility appropriately.
Celebrate their growth.

blocks.text: And point them toward Christ rather than permanent dependence on you.
Then, this week, tell someone one thing God has done for you. Your kids, your wife, a younger man. Say it out loud.
Infrastructure can be inherited. Conviction has to be taught.

Father, thank You for those who invested in us. Forgive us where we have become preoccupied with our own accomplishments. Give us hearts that prepare others. Help us teach truth, share wisdom, and release responsibility faithfully. May the next generation know You, not merely know what we built. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
Infrastructure can be inherited. Conviction has to be taught.
The next generation cannot inherit wisdom we refuse to teach.
Faithful leadership thinks beyond its own tenure.
Point people toward Christ, not permanent dependence on you.
